top_story: Trump’s March threat to destroy Iran’s power plants if Tehran did not reopen the Strait of Hormuz prompted Tehran to warn of regional escalation, and by April 30 markets were already pricing in a prolonged confrontation as oil climbed above $126 on expectations that a U.S. naval blockade could last for months. Trump’s May 2 statement that U.S. strikes on Iran could resume reinforces a coercive posture that keeps the Gulf on edge and raises the risk of broader disruption to shipping, energy costs, and civilian livelihoods far beyond Iran. In Gaza, the supposed US-Israel ceasefire has hardened into a violent and deprivation-driven status quo, with killings, blocked crossings, and collapsing hospitals showing that American military pressure on Iran is unfolding alongside continued tolerance of extreme Palestinian suffering. The emerging picture is of a U.S.-led regional order relying on sustained force and siege, one that is tightening economic shock across the Gulf while deepening humanitarian collapse in Gaza.
